content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Indexing Fundamentals in MongoDB: Single, Compound, and Multikey Indexes"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Indexes support the efficient execution of queries in MongoDB. Without indexes, MongoDB must scan every document in a collection to select those documents that match the query statement. This scan requires MongoDB to process a potentially large amount of data. Indexes are special data structures that store a small portion of the collection's data in an easy-to-traverse form. The index stores the value of a specific field or set of fields, ordered by the value of the field. The ordering of the index entries supports efficient equality matches and range-based query operations. This tutorial covers single, compound, and multikey indexes."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"Single Field Indexes"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"MongoDB supports single field indexes. You can create an index on a single field in a document. The following example creates an index on the 'name' field in the 'users' collection:"},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"db.users.createIndex( { name: 1 } )"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"The value '1' specifies that the index should be created in ascending order. To create an index in descending order, use '-1'."},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"Single field indexes can significantly improve query performance when querying based on that specific field. For example, the following query will benefit from the index created above:"},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"db.users.find( { name: \"John Doe\" } )"},{"order":9,"type":"heading","text":"Compound Indexes"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"MongoDB also supports compound indexes, where an index is created on multiple fields. The order of fields in a compound index is important. The index is sorted based on the first field, then the second, and so on."},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"The following example creates a compound index on the 'age' and 'city' fields in the 'users' collection:"},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"db.users.createIndex( { age: 1, city: 1 } )"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Queries that filter on 'age' and 'city' will benefit from this index. Queries that only filter on 'age' will also benefit, but queries that only filter on 'city' will not effectively use this index. This is because the index is primarily sorted by 'age'."},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider the following queries:"},{"order":15,"type":"code","text":"db.users.find( { age: { $gt: 25 }, city: \"New York\" } ) // Benefits from the index\ndb.users.find( { age: { $gt: 25 } } ) // Benefits from the index\ndb.users.find( { city: \"New York\" } ) // Does NOT effectively use the index"},{"order":16,"type":"heading","text":"Multikey Indexes"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Multikey indexes are used to index array fields. If you index a field that holds an array, MongoDB creates separate index entries for each element of the array."},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, consider a document with an array of tags:"},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"{ _id: ObjectId(\"...\"), name: \"Product A\", tags: [ \"electronics\", \"gadget\", \"new\" ] }"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"To create a multikey index on the 'tags' field, use the following command:"},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"db.products.createIndex( { tags: 1 } )"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Now, queries that search for specific tags will efficiently use the index:"},{"order":23,"type":"code","text":"db.products.find( { tags: \"gadget\" } )"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"MongoDB automatically determines whether to create a multikey index based on the field's data type. You don't need to explicitly specify that you want a multikey index."},{"order":25,"type":"subheading","text":"Considerations for Multikey Indexes"},{"order":26,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Multikey indexes can impact write performance, as each array element requires an index entry."},{"order":27,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Compound indexes can include array fields, but there are limitations on the number of array fields that can be included in a single compound index. Specifically, you can only have one array field in a compound index."},{"order":28,"type":"heading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":29,"type":"paragraph","text":"Understanding the different types of indexes in MongoDB is crucial for optimizing query performance. Single field indexes are suitable for simple queries on a single field, compound indexes are useful for queries involving multiple fields, and multikey indexes are essential for querying array fields. Choosing the right index type can significantly improve the speed and efficiency of your MongoDB applications."}]
